title: What is inbound sales? A plain guide for B2B teams
summary: What is inbound sales? A plain B2B guide: definition, inbound vs outbound, stages and metrics, with Storylane data on what buyers do before they call.
body_markdown:
Ask a sales team when an inbound deal starts and most will point to the form. A visitor asks for a demo, a lead lands in the CRM, an SDR picks it up, and the clock starts.


The buyer's clock started weeks earlier. Storylane's published figure is that[83% of the buying journey happens before sales is contacted](https://www.storylane.io/repx) . So what most teams call "the start of inbound" is closer to the end. The part you don't see is bigger than the part you work, and it decides who gets the call.


## What is inbound sales?


**Inbound sales is selling to buyers who come to you first: they find your company through search, an AI answer, a referral or your content, research you on their own, and then raise their hand.** The seller's job is to help that buyer decide, not to interrupt a stranger.


My definition adds one thing: inbound sales starts when the buyer starts researching, not at the form. Everything in between is part of the sale, even with no rep in it. I call that stretch **the quiet stage** . It overlaps with what marketers call the[dark funnel](https://www.storylane.io/blog/illuminating-dark-funnel) , but it is wider: it includes every visit to your own website before the buyer tells you who they are.


## How is inbound sales different from outbound sales?


Outbound starts with the seller choosing the buyer. Inbound starts with the buyer choosing the seller. That changes almost everything else.


Question Inbound sales Outbound sales


Who makes first contact? The buyer The seller


What the buyer knows at first contact A lot: they have read your site, compared rivals and often formed a view on price Little or nothing about you


The seller's first job Answer well and fast, then qualify Earn attention, then create a reason to talk


What limits volume Demand: traffic, brand, content, AI visibility Rep capacity and list quality


Where deals are lost Before the hand-raise, when the site can't answer, and after it, when follow-up is slow At the first touch, when the message is ignored


Who owns it Marketing and sales together Mostly sales


Most teams run both. If you want the agent-level version of this comparison, see[inbound AI SDRs versus outbound AI SDRs](https://www.storylane.io/blog/inbound-vs-outbound-ai-sdr) .


## Why does the quiet stage matter so much?


Buyers do prefer to research alone, but that doesn't explain what they ask. My theory: asking a website costs the buyer nothing, and asking a salesperson costs them a signal.


The evidence comes from[Storylane's Modern Buying Trends 2026 report](https://www.storylane.io/buyer-experience-report) , which studied 8,211 website agent conversations and 637 deals. Pricing opened 9.4% of conversations with RepX, Storylane's AI website agent, against 2.5% of human sales calls. With a rep, a price question triggers a sequence. On the website it costs nothing, so buyers ask it first.


It also shows who is asking. Across 2,021 recorded calls in 637 mid-market and enterprise deals, about 2.3 of an account's known contacts join an average sales call, and nine in ten of the buying committee never join one. They form their view from the website and whatever gets forwarded (more in[what 637 B2B deals taught us about buying committees](https://www.storylane.io/blog/what-637-b2b-deals-taught-us-about-buying-committees) ).


And it happens when sales is offline: 51.4% of website agent conversations started outside working hours, in the buyer's local time (8,211 conversations across 19 companies). More in[our B2B buyer journey statistics](https://www.storylane.io/blog/b2b-buyer-journey-statistics) .


So the quiet stage is not "pre-sales research". It is the evaluation itself, done by most of the committee, much of it at night, on questions they won't ask a rep yet.


## What do buyers find in the quiet stage?


Often, not enough. The[Storylane Buyability Index](https://buyability-index.storylane.io/) checked 10,580 buyer questions across 529 B2B websites and found that 58.6% got a full answer. Pricing questions did worse, at 46.4%. (The questions are generated per company as what a buyer would plausibly ask, not logged from real buyers, and the sites were chosen by the people who ran the scans.) Often the answer exists but sits[in the docs instead of the pages buyers read](https://www.storylane.io/blog/website-answers-hidden-in-docs) .


This is where inbound pipeline leaks unmeasured. A buyer who can't find an answer doesn't file a ticket. They open the next tab on their shortlist. Full results are in[The 10,580 Questions report](https://www.storylane.io/blog/b2b-buyer-questions-report) .


## What are the stages of inbound sales?


Most stage models begin at "lead". I start one step earlier, where the outcome is set.


1. **The quiet stage.** The buyer finds you, reads, compares and asks the website questions. This is the research part of the[B2B buyer journey](https://www.storylane.io/blog/b2b-buyer-journey) . Owner: marketing and whoever runs the website.
2. **The hand-raise.** A form, a chat, a signup or a meeting request. Owner: demand gen.
3. **Qualification.** Does this buyer fit your ICP, and what do they need? Owner: SDRs, or an agent doing it in conversation. See[real-time lead qualification](https://www.storylane.io/blog/real-time-lead-qualification) .
4. **First response.** How quickly and how well you reply. Owner: sales development. This is where[speed to lead](https://www.storylane.io/blog/what-is-speed-to-lead) matters most.
5. **Evaluation.** Discovery, demo, trial or proof of concept, with more of the committee involved. Owner: AEs and presales.
6. **Decision.** Procurement, security review and sign-off, often by people who never met you. Owner: AEs, with whatever material reaches the approver.


## Which inbound sales metrics should you track?


Track one number per stage, starting with the quiet stage, or nobody will look at it.


Stage Metric What it tells you


Quiet stage Share of real buyer questions your site answers fully Whether buyers can evaluate you without a rep


Hand-raise Visitor to meeting or signup rate, by landing page Which pages turn research into intent


Qualification Share of hand-raises that fit your ICP Whether you are attracting the right buyers


First response Median time to first reply, in and out of working hours Whether interest cools before you answer


Evaluation Meeting to opportunity rate; people reached per account Whether you are selling to the committee or one person


Decision Win rate and cycle length on inbound-sourced deals Whether the whole motion pays off


The first row is the hardest to measure, which is why it gets skipped. If you capture visitor questions through chat or search, count how many got a straight answer. If you don't, that is the first fix.


## Who should own inbound sales?


The common answer is "sales owns it from the lead onward". I disagree: that leaves the quiet stage, which decides the shortlist, owned by nobody. Marketing owns traffic, sales owns meetings, and the questions in between fall through.


I'd give demand gen explicit ownership of the quiet stage, measured on answer coverage and hand-raise rate, not just leads. Sales then owns everything from the hand-raise, measured on response time and conversion.


## How do you sell in the quiet stage?


You can't put a rep on every visit at 11pm. You can make sure the site answers what a rep would. Three moves, in order of effort:


- **Put the answers where buyers start.** Pricing logic, setup time, integrations and security belong on the pages buyers land on, not only in the docs. Start with a clear[pricing page](https://www.storylane.io/blog/saas-pricing-page-design) .
- **Show the product.** An interactive demo answers "how does it actually work" for the committee members who never join a call, and it can be forwarded.
- **Answer in conversation.** An AI website agent takes the questions buyers won't ask a rep and qualifies them while it answers. It also changes when buyers share details: in[Storylane's Modern Buying Trends 2026 report](https://www.storylane.io/buyer-experience-report) , 1% of buyers gave an email after one message to a website agent, and 31% did after five or six. That is the opposite of[a contact form that asks first](https://www.storylane.io/blog/why-contact-forms-suppress-conversion) .


This is where I have a bias: Storylane builds the third option.[RepX](https://www.storylane.io/repx) is a website agent best for teams whose inbound traffic arrives with real product questions. It answers in text, voice or video, pulls up[interactive demos inside the conversation](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/training-repx/demos-images-and-videos) , qualifies against an ICP you describe in plain English, handles objections within guardrails you set, and books meetings.[Playbooks](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/playbooks/introduction-to-playbooks) let each page behave differently: its own starter questions, qualification questions, rule for when to ask for an email, and goal, such as booking a meeting or starting a trial. Qualified leads and conversation summaries flow to HubSpot, Salesforce and Slack. Hospitable[booked 36 meetings and closed 7 deals in its first month with RepX](https://www.storylane.io/customer-stories/how-hospitable-booked-36-meetings-in-a-month-with-repx) . RepX starts at $2,000 a month, and the price depends on website traffic. Whatever tool you pick, the job is the same: be present in the quiet stage.


Next, make the hand-raise and follow-up feel built for each buyer: see[how to build a personalized inbound sales strategy](https://www.storylane.io/blog/personalized-inbound-sales-strategy) .


## What to do on Monday


Remember one idea: inbound sales starts when the buyer starts, and most of it happens in the quiet stage, before anyone on your team knows the buyer exists.


On Monday, write down the ten questions a buyer in your category asks before talking to sales. Answer each one from your own website, starting from the page they would land on. Every question you can't answer in two clicks is a deal you may be losing without ever seeing it.
